---
title: "Branching and Writing"
---

Pinning makes the past reproducible. *Branching* makes the present safe to
change: `tether new -b NAME` starts a bookmark and, with it, a branch named
after it in every system off the pinned state; you write through native
handles; `commit` pins the results and moves the bookmark. Nothing you do on a
bookmark touches `main` in any system until you `promote` it.

This walkthrough continues from [Pinning](03-pinning.qmd) and adds a Lance
feature store and the analysis code itself as objects, so the recipe covers
four different systems.

## Register a few more objects

```bash
tether add features --kind lance s3://bucket/features.lance
tether add code     --kind git ../analysis-code --remote origin
tether commit -m "Add feature store and code"
```

`code` pins a *separate* git repository -- the analysis code -- at its `HEAD`
sha (as a tag), so a dataset commit also names the code that produced it. Do
not register the repository the dataset itself lives in: every `tether commit`
moves its sha, so every trunk `pull` would find it moved and re-pin it forever.

## A bookmark is a branch in every system: `tether new -b`

`init` left the working copy on the trunk bookmark, `main`. There, every
object's working ref is its *upstream* branch -- `main` in Icechunk, `main`
in Neon -- and `commit` pins wherever those are. To work without touching
them, start a bookmark:

```bash
tether new -b relabel
```

```
on bookmark relabel; working refs set up
  code          -> tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.relabel  (created on first writable open)
  db/metrics    -> tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.relabel  (created on first writable open)
  features      -> tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.relabel  (created on first writable open)
  zarr/imaging  -> tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.relabel  (created on first writable open)
```

`jj log` now shows a `relabel` bookmark where `main` is, and every Forkable
system will get a `tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.relabel` branch: the same name on both
sides, so `jj log` and `icechunk branch list` tell one story. `new` decided
the names and where they fork from -- the pins at `main` -- and wrote nothing.
Forking is **lazy** by default: the branch is created by the first writable
`open` of that object. A bookmark that reads three objects and writes one ends
up with one branch, not four.

| Object | Pin at `main` | Branch for `relabel` (created on first write) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `zarr/imaging` | Icechunk tag | Icechunk branch `tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.relabel` |
| `db/metrics` | Neon branch | Neon child branch `tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.relabel` |
| `features` | Lance tag | Lance branch `tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.relabel` |
| `code` | git tag | git branch `tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.relabel` |

`0a1b2c3d` is the dataset's id (from `tether.toml`), so two datasets sharing
a store never collide. Objects sharing one system share the branch: it is the
system's branch, not the object's. `raw/plate1` has no working ref: files
cannot be forked. `tether new relabel` from another checkout joins the
bookmark -- refused while this checkout works on it, unless `--shared`, since
both would write the same branches. `tether new main` returns to the trunk;
`tether new REV` for a revision carrying no bookmark gives a read-only working
copy (`open --rev`, `status`, `verify` work; writes need a bookmark).

`status` reads objects that have not been forked yet at their base (the pin),
and all are `clean`; once a branch exists, `status` reads it instead.

### Lazy or eager

`tether new --eager` (or `[new] fork = "eager"` in `tether.toml`) creates every
branch during `new`, which is how tether worked before 0.1.0a6. Every fork in
every backend is a copy-on-write pointer, so the difference is not the cost of
creating a branch; it is what an idle branch *holds* and *needs*:

| | Lazy (default) | Eager |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Branches created | only for objects you actually write | one per Forkable object, every `new` |
| What a forgotten workspace leaves behind | nothing for untouched objects | a branch per object -- each a GC root that keeps its snapshot alive and a line in every branch list; Neon counts them against the project's branch quota |
| Credentials needed at `new` | read only | write, for every system |
| First writable `open` | pays the fork (one metadata write, plus a cheap pin check) | just opens |
| `--dry-run` | `new --dry-run` shows `defer-fork`; the fork itself happens inside `open`, which has no dry run -- use `new --eager --dry-run` to preview what would be created | `new --dry-run` shows every `fork` |
| HEAD moves before you write | the workspace is stale; `new` re-decides with nothing to reset | `new` resets the branches |
| The pin is deleted before you write (`gc` on another machine) | `open` fails with `pin missing` -- the fork never happened | the branch already exists and keeps the data |
| Pre-creating branches for a job | `Repo.materialize_fork(key)` per object, or `--eager` | automatic |

If one system refuses to fork (quota, network), `new` still records the
branches it did create and names the object that failed; run `new` again once
the cause is gone -- existing branches are reset onto the pin, never
duplicated.

The last two rows are the same trade-off: a pin is durable, so deferring the
fork is safe as long as the pin outlives the wait -- which it does unless
someone drops the commit that references it and runs `gc` in between.

**Pin-less objects are never deferred.** With `--pin record` there is no tag;
the recorded state is a bare snapshot id / version / commit / LSN that the
system will eventually expire (Icechunk `expire_snapshots`, Iceberg snapshot
expiry, Lance `cleanup_old_versions`, Neon's history window). A branch on it is
the only thing that stops that. So `new` forks those immediately even in lazy
mode -- the plan says `fork ... forked now so the state cannot expire` -- and
the trade-off above does not apply to them.

## Write through native handles

`open` without `-r` returns a **writable** handle for Forkable objects,
positioned on the working ref. tether hands you the system's own objects and
gets out of the way.

### Icechunk

```python
import zarr
from tether import Repo
from tether.handles import IcechunkHandle

repo = Repo.find(".")
h = repo.open("zarr/imaging")
assert isinstance(h, IcechunkHandle) and not h.read_only
print(h.branch)                       # tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.relabel

group = zarr.open_group(h.session.store, mode="a")
group["labels"][...] = relabel(group["labels"][...])
h.session.commit("Relabel plate1 with model v3")   # an Icechunk commit on the fork
```

### Lance

```python
import lance, pyarrow as pa
from tether.handles import LanceHandle

h = repo.open("features")
assert isinstance(h, LanceHandle)
lance.write_dataset(pa.table({"well": ["A1"], "score": [0.91]}), h.dataset, mode="append")
```

### Neon (any Postgres client)

```python
import psycopg
from tether.handles import NeonHandle

h = repo.open("db/metrics")
assert isinstance(h, NeonHandle)
with psycopg.connect(h.url) as conn:     # URL for the forked branch's endpoint
    conn.execute("INSERT INTO metrics (well, score) VALUES ('A1', 0.91)")
```

Opening a Neon fork writable creates a `read_write` compute endpoint on the
branch if none exists; the URL points at it.

::: {.callout-note title="Neon: pins are children of the branch they were taken on"}
A Neon pin is a branch at an LSN, and a pin taken on your working branch is a
*child* of it. That shapes what `new` and `gc` can do afterwards:

- `commit` then `new` keeps your working branch: it already sits at the state
  that was just pinned from it, so the plan says `reuse` and nothing is reset.
- `new` onto a *different* pin (the bookmark moved by hand to an older
  commit) cannot reset a branch that has pin children -- Neon will not
  restore it in place -- so the fork lands on a sibling name
  (`...relabel.2`) and the old branch stays as the pins' parent. Your
  workspace records the sibling.
- Neither `gc --prune-bookmarks` nor `--force-prune` can delete a branch
  while pins hang off it; the plan lists it as `keep-branch: cannot be
  deleted` with the pins named. Release those pins first (drop the commits
  that reference them, `gc`), then the branch goes.

Icechunk, Iceberg, Lance, lakeFS, and Dolt pins are tags or independent refs,
so none of this applies to them.
:::

### Code

```python
from tether.handles import GitHandle

h = repo.open("code")
assert isinstance(h, GitHandle)
h.sha, h.path        # the fork branch's head; commit your code changes there
```

From the shell, `tether open <key>` prints the same addresses:

```bash
tether open db/metrics
postgresql://runner@ep-brisk-forest-x9y8z7.us-west-2.aws.neon.tech/metrics?...
tether open features
s3://bucket/features.lance#tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.relabel@v4
```

## See what changed

```bash
tether status --snapshot
```

```
dataset 3ba1c07e55d2
  modified  code  [git/forkable]
  modified  db/metrics  [neon/forkable]
  modified  features  [lance/forkable]
     clean  raw/plate1  [file/observed] unrecoverable
  modified  zarr/imaging  [icechunk/forkable]
```

`diff` with no arguments compares the current commit's manifests with the
working tree; nothing has been recorded yet, so use `--content` after the
commit below. Meanwhile `main` in every system is untouched: the forks isolate
your work.

## Commit: pin the branches, move the bookmark

```bash
tether commit -m "Relabel plate1 with model v3; scores for A1"
```

```
  pinned code -> tether.0a1b2c3d.f01a9d3c2b7ee5f6
  pinned db/metrics -> tether.0a1b2c3d.55e2ab7d9c10e5f6
  pinned features -> tether.0a1b2c3d.9e7c4b2f0a61e5f6
  pinned zarr/imaging -> tether.0a1b2c3d.deb4861eb388e5f6
committed 41c0d9e2b7f3
```

Each pin points at the state of the bookmark's *branch*: an Icechunk tag on
the branch's snapshot, a Lance tag on `(branch, version)`, a Neon branch at
the branch's LSN, a git tag on the branch's sha. Then the manifests were
committed and the `relabel` bookmark moved onto the commit -- in one jj
operation, so `jj undo` takes both back. `main` (the bookmark and every
system's `main`) has not moved. Now compare:

```bash
tether diff main @- --content
```

```
    changed  code  [+0 -0 ~1 files]
               modified  segment.py  +12 -3
    changed  db/metrics
    changed  features  [+1 -0 ~0 fragments]
                  added  fragment 4  +1 rows
    changed  zarr/imaging  [+0 -0 ~1 nodes]
               modified  /labels  12 chunks
```

Continue writing on the same branches and committing as often as you like;
each commit pins the latest state and moves the bookmark, and the previous
pins stay valid (they are what `open -r` and `verify` use). `commit` is not
`jj commit`: it starts nothing new, and the next write lands on the same
branches.

## Landing it: `tether promote`

Your dataset commit pins the bookmark's state in every system. To land it --
make each system's *upstream branch* point at that state, then move the
trunk bookmark to your commit; `jj bookmark set main -r relabel`, for data --
run:

```bash
tether promote --dry-run
```

```
plan: promote (3 write(s))
        fast-forward  code          [git] main  main sha=41c0d9e2b7f3… -> sha=f01a9d3c2b7e… (base unchanged since fork)
        fast-forward  features      [lance] main  ...
        fast-forward  zarr/imaging  [icechunk] main  main snapshot_id=K3F9M2A1B7C8… -> snapshot_id=DEB4861EB388… (base unchanged since fork)
              refuse  db/metrics    [neon] main  the neon backend cannot move a branch; Neon cannot promote a child branch into its parent; work on the trunk bookmark ...
```

For each Forkable object tether compares the upstream branch to the **fork
point** -- the state recorded in `workspace.toml` when the branch was created
-- and decides:

| Upstream since your fork | Backend has | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| unchanged | `PROMOTE` | **fast-forward**: upstream is moved to the branch's head; nothing is rewritten |
| moved | `MERGE` | **merge**: the system's own three-way merge (lakeFS `merge_into`, Dolt `DOLT_MERGE`, `git merge`); conflicts are reported and nothing is written |
| moved | `PROMOTE` only | **refuse**, with the system's recipe (Icechunk and Iceberg have no merge) |
| anything | neither | **refuse** (Neon, Lance) |

`--strategy ff` refuses anything that is not a fast-forward -- the setting for
CI, where a surprise merge is worse than a failure. `--strategy merge` refuses
plain fast-forwards when you want a merge commit for the record. `--rev REV`
promotes what a *dataset commit* pinned instead of this bookmark's live
branches (the ancestry check replaces the fork point; the trunk bookmark is
not moved). `--dry-run`, `--plan`, and `--from-plan` work as everywhere else;
apply refuses if an upstream moved after the plan was made.

When everything **fast-forwarded** and nothing was refused, the trunk bookmark
moves to your commit: the manifests there already name the states upstream
now holds. After a **merge** upstream holds a state no commit has pinned yet,
so `promote` resets your branch onto the merge result and leaves the trunk
where it is; `tether commit` pins the merge, and a second `promote` is then a
fast-forward that moves it.

```bash
tether promote                                       # fast-forward what it can, merge where the system can
tether commit -m "Merge plate1 relabel into main"    # only after a merge
tether promote                                       # ...then this moves main
```

Refusals are the honest part -- and they hold everything else back. A
bookmark lands whole or not at all: when one system is refused, `promote`
reports the others as `held` (with what each would have done) and writes
nothing, because a `main` with the new state in one system and the old in
another is the half-done state you branched to avoid. Name keys to land a
subset on purpose (`tether promote zarr/imaging`); the trunk bookmark never
moves for a subset, so `main` keeps pointing at a commit that describes
upstream. Icechunk and Iceberg can fast-forward but not
merge; if upstream moved under you, re-apply the writes on a fresh bookmark
(or, for Icechunk, `reset_branch` when discarding `main`'s newer snapshots is
what you mean). Lance cannot move a branch head at all yet. Neon cannot
promote a child branch into its parent -- for a database that must receive
writes on `main`, work on the trunk bookmark, where the working ref *is*
`main` and pins (child branches at an LSN) provide reproducibility.

## Positions, and `tether pull`

A dataset commit records an exact state per object. Between commits each
object has a *position* -- what the next commit will record -- and it works
the way files do in a VCS: what you did not touch stays exactly as the last
commit had it.

- On the **trunk**, a Forkable object's position is its upstream branch head:
  `commit` fingerprints it and pins whatever is there.
- On another **bookmark**, its position is the bookmark's branch once that
  exists; until the first write it sits at the pin the bookmark started from,
  and `commit` does not contact it.
- Objects whose system has **no branches** (files, Iceberg, Delta, DuckLake)
  sit at their pin on every bookmark. So does an object registered `--at`,
  until a trunk `pull` moves it onto the branch.
- An object with **no commit yet** is read once, at the branch head or at
  `--at`.

`tether pull` is the fetch: it reads the heads of the bookmark's branches and
commits what moved onto the bookmark. On the trunk that means every upstream
branch and every branch-less object -- a table's current version, a
directory's contents -- so a nightly `tether pull` on `main` is the dataset
trailing the world:

```bash
tether new main
tether pull
```

```
  pulled zarr/imaging  snapshot_id=TYZ25DJEHXER -> snapshot_id=AZ1REKMV3HET
  pulled raw/plate1  digest=9f2e1c… -> digest=0b7a4d…
  up to date db/metrics
committed 8d5719841a09 on main
```

Nothing moved: no commit. A `file = "immutable"` object that changed is
refused, as `status --snapshot` refuses it: accepting a new state is a
re-registration, not a pull. `undo` uncommits a pull like a commit (the pins
stay). On a feature bookmark the branches *are* the working refs, so `pull`
and `commit` see the same heads; objects with no branch yet are skipped.

`status --snapshot` on the trunk shows what a pull would take: `modified` for
upstream branches that moved, `behind` for branch-less objects and `--at`
positions.

### Starting from an older snapshot

`--at` sets an object's *initial* position: a state that was never pinned --
an older Icechunk snapshot from before you adopted tether, a Lance version, a
Dolt or lakeFS commit. `tether log` shows what there is to choose from, with
each system's own ids, timestamps, and messages, and marks branches, tags,
and tether pins:

```bash
tether log zarr/imaging                         # a registered object
tether log s3://bucket/imaging.icechunk --kind icechunk   # before registering
```

```
  AZ1REKMV3HETD2X7EW7G  2026-09-05 15:16  Relabel plate1 with model v3  [main]
  TYZ25DJEHXERGBR7H3P0  2026-09-05 14:02  Segment plate1
  M32R7C6M4H4Y8BEGSEK0  2026-09-05 13:40  Convert plate1
  1CECHNKREP0F1RSTCMT0  2026-09-05 13:39  Repository initialized
```

```bash
tether add zarr/imaging --kind icechunk s3://bucket/imaging.icechunk --at TYZ25DJEHXERGBR7H3P0
tether commit -m "Adopt imaging at the pre-relabel snapshot"
tether new -b from-pre-relabel
```

`--pick` does the same interactively -- it prints the list numbered and asks
which entry to use:

```bash
tether add zarr/imaging --kind icechunk s3://bucket/imaging.icechunk --pick
```

```
  1. AZ1REKMV3HETD2X7EW7G  2026-09-05 15:16  Relabel plate1 with model v3  [main]
  2. TYZ25DJEHXERGBR7H3P0  2026-09-05 14:02  Segment plate1
  3. M32R7C6M4H4Y8BEGSEK0  2026-09-05 13:40  Convert plate1
  4. 1CECHNKREP0F1RSTCMT0  2026-09-05 13:39  Repository initialized
Pick an entry (number or id) [1]: 2
added zarr/imaging (icechunk) at TYZ25DJEHXERGBR7H3P0
```

The first `commit` pins that state, `open` reads it, and a bookmark forks
from the pin, exactly as if it had been the branch head. After that `at` has
no further role: the pin is the position, and a trunk `tether pull` moves the
object onto `main` (dropping `at` from the manifest). The ids `tether log`
prints are always valid `at` values; the per-system forms are in the
[backends guide](09-backends.qmd). Neon and files have no `at`.

## Working on the trunk

Some objects should never be forked -- a production database, a shared
`main` you deliberately advance. That is what the trunk bookmark is for:

```bash
tether new main
tether open db/prod        # a writable handle to main itself
tether commit -m "Nightly load"
```

On the trunk every Forkable object's working ref is its upstream branch
(`locator.branch`, `main` by default; `[vcs] trunk` names the bookmark).
`open` returns a writable handle to it and `commit` pins whatever state it
finds there, so you get reproducibility without branch sprawl; the Neon
quiescence check (`commit` refuses while writers are active unless `--force`)
keeps pins consistent. Two checkouts may both work on the trunk -- that is
what a shared `main` means -- where any other bookmark is refused to a second
checkout unless `--shared`.

## Stale working copies

If an object's committed manifest changes under you -- a teammate committed
it on the same bookmark (`--shared`), or the bookmark was moved by hand to a
revision where it is pinned differently -- your branch was forked from a state
that is no longer the dataset's:

```bash
tether status
```

```
dataset 9d0e5f71ac22 (STALE: zarr/imaging)
  ...
```

```bash
tether open zarr/imaging
error: working copy is stale: the committed state of zarr/imaging changed since this workspace forked; run `tether new` to refork before writing
```

Staleness is per object: the other forks stay writable, your own commits never
make you stale, and adding or removing unrelated objects does not clear it.

`tether new` re-decides from the current pins and clears the flag. Everything
you *committed* is safe: those pins are tags, independent of any branch. Writes
you did not commit are not: re-forking an existing branch resets it to the new
pin (Icechunk `reset_branch`, Lance/lakeFS/Dolt delete-and-recreate, git
`branch -f`, Neon branch restore). `new` therefore looks at every branch it
would reset first, and refuses if one holds writes beyond what you last
committed:

```
$ tether new
error: refusing to reset working branches with unpinned writes:
  zarr/imaging: tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.relabel has writes since this workspace last committed (snapshot_id=Q7ZK…); commit them, or pass --discard to throw them away
```

Commit, or `tether new --discard` if that was scratch work. Branches that
were still pending are simply re-decided; there was nothing to reset.

## Undo

Every command that touched a store is in this workspace's operation log:

```bash
tether ops
```

```
9f2e1c7b3a5d  2026-09-05T10:41:12+00:00  commit   pinned zarr/imaging, db/metrics; vcs 4c1e2a9b7d3f
3f1c9a2b7d4e  2026-09-05T10:22:03+00:00  fork     forked zarr/imaging -> tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.relabel
b7d4e3f1c9a2  2026-09-05T10:21:55+00:00  new      deferred code, db/metrics, features, zarr/imaging; on relabel
```

`tether undo` reverses the newest entry where the store still allows it. Undo
the commit and it is *uncommitted*: the dataset commit leaves the VCS, the
manifests are working-tree changes again, and the pins stay -- they are still
referenced, so `gc` keeps them and `tether commit` re-records them. Undo the
fork and the branch is deleted (refused, like `new`, if it gained writes you
never committed -- `--discard` overrides) and `workspace.toml` goes back to
saying the fork is pending. Undo the `new` and the working copy returns to
where it was, too.

```bash
tether undo            # the commit -> uncommitted; pins kept
tether undo            # the fork  -> branch deleted, fork pending again
tether ops             # both entries now read "(undone by ...)"
```

What undo cannot do it says so: a `gc` that deleted pins gets its branches
and listings back but reports the pins as `IRREVERSIBLE` (exit code 2); a
`promote` is refused with the previous base heads printed. `jj undo` and
`git reset` stay what they were -- they move the manifests, never the stores;
tether's undo is the other half.

If a store lost something a manifest promises -- a pin deleted by hand, a
branch this workspace expects -- `tether repair` recreates it from the recorded
state, while the store still has that state.

## Workspaces and bookmarks

Each jj workspace (or each checkout) is its own tether workspace, with its own
untracked `.tether/workspace.toml` saying which bookmark it works on. Two
checkouts on two bookmarks never write the same store branch. Two checkouts on
*one* bookmark would, so `tether new NAME` refuses a bookmark another live
checkout holds unless you pass `--shared` -- a choice, not a default. The
trunk is the exception: `main` is shared by nature.

When the VCS moves a bookmark behind tether's back -- `jj bookmark delete`,
`jj bookmark rename`, `jj bookmark set` to another commit, or a `jj new` that
leaves it -- `tether status` says so, with what to do: `tether new NAME` to
return or continue under the new name, `tether new -b NAME` to recreate one,
`gc --prune-bookmarks` to release the branches of a bookmark that is gone.

## Recap

- `tether new -b NAME [rev]` starts a bookmark and, per Forkable object, a
  branch named after it (`tether.ws.<dataset>.NAME`) off the pins at `rev`;
  created on the first writable `open` (`--eager` creates them all now;
  `--pin record` objects always fork now). `tether new NAME` joins one;
  `tether new main` works on the trunk, where the working refs are the
  upstream branches; no bookmark means read-only.
- `open` returns writable native handles on those branches; write with the
  system's own library.
- `commit` pins the branches' states, commits the manifests, and moves the
  bookmark; `diff --content` shows what changed inside each system.
- `promote` moves each system's upstream branch to the bookmark's branch --
  fast-forward when unchanged since the fork point, native merge where the
  system has one, refusal with the system's recipe otherwise -- then moves the
  trunk bookmark to the commit.
- `pull` on the trunk reads every upstream branch and branch-less object and
  commits what moved.
